## Ezra 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "By the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people assembled as one man in Jerusalem."

- **Timing.** The "seventh month" is Tishri (September/October), the most sacred month in Israel's calendar, containing the Feast of Trumpets (day 1), the Day of Atonement (day 10), and the Feast of Tabernacles (days 15–22). The phrase "when the seventh month was come" may more precisely mean "was approaching" — the people gathered before the month actually arrived so that the altar could be ready for the first day's sacrifices. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **"As one man."** This Hebrew idiom denotes remarkable unity of mind and heart — the gathering was universal and carried out with the dispatch as if only one person were involved. Gill suggests it may even imply a divine impulse, "without any consultation, or knowledge of each other's designs." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm; Precept Austin citing Utley: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)
- **Practical context.** The return from Babylon likely occurred in the spring; the people first settled in their towns and repaired dwellings, then traveled to Jerusalem for the seventh-month feasts as the Law required (Exodus 23:14–16). (Pulpit Commentary Homiletics: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/ezra/3.htm)
- **Historical note.** Henry Morris suggests this gathering and the reinstitution of sacrifices "probably marks the end of the seventy-year exile predicted by Jeremiah" (Jer 25:11–12; Dan 9:2), with the exile beginning c. 605 BC and return c. 535 BC. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — "Then Jeshua son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and his associates, began to build the altar of the God of Israel to sacrifice burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God."

- **The two leaders.** Jeshua (or Joshua) was the high priest — grandson of Seraiah, the last high priest before the exile who was executed by Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 25:18, 21). Zerubbabel was the civil governor (prince) of Judah, a descendant of David. Both were essential: Jeshua to give the priestly lead, Zerubbabel to give civil authority and encouragement. (Enduring Word citing Clarke: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **The altar first.** The altar was built as the beginning of the work — the temple would later be built around it as the centre of all. It was the place where sin was dealt with and where ordinary Israelites met God (the temple interior was restricted to priests). Building the altar first was a wise spiritual priority, showing the people understood their need for atonement and dedication. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **A point repeatedly stressed by commentators:** "There cannot be a temple without an altar, but there may be an altar without a temple. God meets men at the place of sacrifice, even though there be no house for His name." (Enduring Word citing Maclaren: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Obedience to the Word.** The phrase "as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God" emphasizes they were not innovating but strictly following the Pentateuch (e.g., Exodus 27:1–8; Leviticus 1). Steven Cole notes they "didn't take a poll" or pursue contemporary innovations but "went back to the Word of God and they obeyed it." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **"Moses the man of God."** This title for Moses is noted as paralleling the later use of "man of God" for David (Neh 12:24, 36). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)

---

### v. 3 — "They set up the altar on its foundation and sacrificed burnt offerings on it to the LORD—both the morning and evening burnt offerings—even though they feared the people of the land."

- **"On its foundation" (KJV: "upon his bases").** The altar was deliberately placed on the old site, the ancient foundations discovered among the ruins. This signified continuity — all the new was to be a restoration of the old. The site dated back to David's altar on the threshing floor of Araunah (2 Samuel 24:16–19). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **"Even though they feared" (KJV: "for fear was upon them").** Two interpretations appear among the commentators:
  - *Fear as motivation:* Their fear of the surrounding peoples drove them to seek God's protection. Before the altar was built and offerings made, they "did not feel sure of the Divine protection." The act of building the altar was "their first act of defiance in the presence of the nations around." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rebuilding-the-temple)
  - *Fear notwithstanding:* Alternatively, some render it "though fear was upon them" — they were not deterred from worship despite their fear. (Gill citing Junius & Tremellius: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **Spiritual protection.** Maclaren observes: "The ruined Jerusalem was better guarded by that altar than if its fallen walls had been rebuilt." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Morning and evening sacrifices.** These resumed immediately, as prescribed in Exodus 29:38–42 and Numbers 28:1–8 — the daily tamid offerings. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)

---

### v. 4 — "They also celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written, and they offered burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day."

- **The Feast of Tabernacles (Sukkot).** This began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Lev 23:34) and lasted eight days. It celebrated God's faithfulness during the wilderness wanderings, with families living in temporary shelters (booths). For returned exiles who were themselves living in makeshift conditions among ruined cities, this feast held special poignancy. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **"In accordance with what is written."** Another stress on strict obedience to the Mosaic instructions. The prescribed daily numbers of sacrifices followed Numbers 29:13–34 — thirteen oxen on day one, twelve on day two, and so on, diminishing each day. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm; Keil & Delitzsch via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-3.html)
- **The whole Mosaic economy of service was being restored.** Ellicott notes that the intention of these verses "is to lay stress on the provision made for an entire renewal of the Mosaic economy." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)

---

### v. 5 — "After that, they presented the regular burnt offerings and those for New Moons and for all the appointed sacred feasts of the LORD, as well as all the freewill offerings brought to the LORD."

- **Comprehensive restoration.** This verse is "general and anticipatory" — it looks forward to the full round of Israel's liturgical calendar. After the Feast of Tabernacles, they continued with the daily offerings, the New Moon offerings (first day of each month, Num 28:11–15), the three annual pilgrimage feasts, and the freewill offerings individuals brought. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Keil & Delitzsch via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-3.html)
- **Freewill offerings.** Individuals could bring burnt offerings from free inclination on any day, but they were especially presented at the annual festivals after the prescribed sacrifices (Num 29:39). (Keil & Delitzsch: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezra-3.html)
- **All this occurred before the temple was built**, which commentators find theologically significant: "The worship itself is felt to be more important than the house in which it is to be celebrated." (Enduring Word citing Adeney: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)

---

### v. 6 — "On the first day of the seventh month, the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD, although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid."

- **Chronology.** The altar was completed before the first day of the seventh month (the Feast of Trumpets / New Year). From the first to the fifteenth (when Tabernacles began), the daily sacrifice was offered. This verse recapitulates the timeline and its second half provides the transition to the temple construction narrative. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **The Day of Atonement.** Gill notes that although not explicitly mentioned, the tenth day of this month (the Day of Atonement, Lev 23:27) was certainly also observed "with all the rites of it." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **Contrast.** The verse highlights that true worship of God resumed even while the temple itself remained in ruins — sacrifice before structure, altar before architecture. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)

---

### v. 7 — "They gave money to the masons and carpenters, and food and drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea, as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia."

- **Gentile cooperation.** Just as Solomon had done for the first temple (1 Kings 5; 2 Chron 2), they contracted with the Phoenicians (Sidon and Tyre) to supply cedar from Lebanon. Jewish workmen (masons and carpenters) were paid in money; the Phoenicians were paid in kind — food, drink, and oil — because such commodities were scarcer in their territory. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Cedar from Lebanon.** These were the legendary timbers used in Solomon's temple, showing the people's determination to use the best materials despite their poverty. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Joppa.** The nearest seaport to Jerusalem, about 35–40 miles inland. The logs were floated down the coast from Phoenicia to Joppa, then hauled overland to Jerusalem. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **"Authorized" (KJV: "grant").** Kidner suggests the word implies more than mere permission — it includes financial provision, "as with our own word 'grant.'" (Enduring Word citing Kidner: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Gill's note on Cyrus's authority.** Since Tyre and Sidon were under Persian dominion, Cyrus not only permitted the Jews to obtain cedar but ordered the Phoenicians to furnish it for a fair price. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)

---

### v. 8 — "In the second month of the second year after they had arrived at the house of God in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the rest of their associates including the priests, the Levites, and all who had returned to Jerusalem from the captivity, began the work. They appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD."

- **The second month of the second year.** The second month (Ziv/Iyar, April/May) of the second year of Cyrus — about 536 BC. Ellicott and Kidner both note this was the very month Solomon had begun building the first temple (1 Kings 6:1). The parallel would not have escaped the people; they were deliberately patterning their restoration after Solomon's. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Winter pause.** Gill explains the chronology: after the Feast of Tabernacles in the seventh month, the people returned to their cities through the winter (an improper season for building). They left workers to clear rubble and prepare materials, then resumed in the spring after Passover. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **Levites from twenty years.** The Mosaic Law originally set Levitical service at age thirty (Num 4:1–3). David later reduced it to twenty (1 Chron 23:24). Under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, they adopted David's revised standard — "in strict harmony with the original ordinances of David." This shows their care to follow Scriptural precedent. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **"The house of God."** The site is called "the house of God at Jerusalem" even before the temple was built and while the former temple was still a ruin — emphasizing the sanctity of the location itself. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
- **Gill's note on Sheshbazzar.** The absence of reference to Sheshbazzar (cf. Ezra 1:8, 11) may indicate he had died or passed from the scene. (Constable via StudyLight search result)

---

### v. 9 — "So Jeshua and his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons (descendants of Yehudah), and the sons of Henadad and their sons and brothers—all Levites—joined together to supervise those working on the house of God."

- **Jeshua the Levite.** Gill clarifies that this Jeshua is not the high priest of v. 2 but a Levite listed in Ezra 2:40 (along with Kadmiel). (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **Unanimity.** Ellicott notes that Jeshua and Kadmiel were both of the stock of Judah (or Hodaviah, Ezra 2:40; Hodevah, Neh 7:43), the two heads of Levitical families. "Their fewness is compensated by their unanimity and vigour." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **Henadad** is not listed in Ezra 2:40 but appears as a Levitical name in Nehemiah. The reason for the difference is not possible to determine. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **"Joined together" (KJV: "as one").** The same note of unity that appeared in v. 1. The Levitical supervisors worked in single-minded coordination. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)

---

### v. 10 — "When the builders had laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites (the sons of Asaph) with cymbals, took their positions to praise the LORD, as David king of Israel had prescribed."

- **The ceremonial.** As soon as the foundation was laid, a formal worship service was conducted. The priests stood "in their apparel" (priestly vestments) with trumpets; the Levites (specifically the sons of Asaph, the musical guild) with cymbals. The trumpets belonged to the priests and the cymbals to the Levites in the ancient ordinances. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **"After the ordinance of David."** David had organized temple music and worship (1 Chron 6, 15:16, 16:25). Everything went back to earlier precedents: the sacrifices were "according to the Law of Moses" and the musical ceremonial "according to the ordinance of David." The restoration was anchored in continuity. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Gaebelein via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezra-3.html)
- **Humble circumstances.** The general description matches the massive dedication ceremony for Solomon's temple (2 Chron 5:13), but this was held in far humbler circumstances — "this time there is no ark, no visible glory, indeed no Temple; only some beginnings, and small beginnings at that. But God is enthroned on the praises of Israel, and these could be as glorious as Solomon's." (Enduring Word citing Kidner: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)

---

### v. 11 — "And they sang responsively with praise and thanksgiving to the LORD: 'For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever.' Then all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid."

- **Responsive (antiphonal) singing.** They sang "by course" (KJV) — answering one another in chorus, likely in two groups alternating. The word used implies a back-and-forth pattern of praise. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **"For He is good; for His loving devotion endures forever."** This refrain appears repeatedly in Psalm 136 (each verse) and was used at Solomon's temple dedication (2 Chron 5:13; 7:3). It may be that Psalm 136 was the very psalm sung responsively. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **The great shout.** A corporate acclamation of praise — the entire assembly erupted in shouting "because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid." Constable notes principles of praise here: "Praise is the act of publicly exalting God's person and work… Praise is a participating activity, not a spectator sport." (Constable via StudyLight search; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)

---

### v. 12 — "But many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple. Still, many others shouted joyfully."

- **Who wept.** "Ancient men" — priests, Levites, and heads of families who were old enough to remember Solomon's temple. The first temple was destroyed in 586 BC, only about 50 years before this event. Those 70–80 years old would have clear memories of its glory. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **Why they wept.** Multiple reasons converged:
  - The new temple's foundation was visibly smaller and humbler than Solomon's. (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rebuilding-the-temple)
  - The second temple lacked the ark of the covenant, the heavenly fire, the mercy seat, the Shekinah glory, the Urim and Thummim, and the spirit of prophecy. (Enduring Word citing Clarke: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
  - "Possibly some of them had stood on this very spot half a century before, in an agony of despair, while they saw the cruel flames licking the ancient stones." (Enduring Word citing Adeney: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)
  - Ellicott says the weeping was "not occasioned by any comparison as to size and grandeur" primarily but "they thought chiefly of the great desolation as measured by the past." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **Who rejoiced.** The younger generation, who had never seen the first temple, felt nothing but joy at this important step forward. They had known only the misery of having no temple at all; to them even this foundation seemed great. (Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezra/3.htm)
- **Prophetic context.** The prophets Haggai and Zechariah later addressed this despair about the humble new temple (Hag 2:1–9; Zech 4:8–10). Haggai 2:3 explicitly asks, "Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not in your eyes as nothing?" Yet Haggai promised, "The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former" (Hag 2:9) — fulfilled when Jesus Christ Himself entered this very temple. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)

---

### v. 13 — "The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise. And the sound was heard from afar."

- **Joy and sorrow blended.** The weeping and the shouting were so mingled that one could not tell them apart — "the rejoicing and the sorrow were blended, and the common sound was heard from far." Ellicott adds, "All here has the stamp of truth" — the psychological realism of the scene speaks to its authenticity. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezra/3.htm)
- **Which sound carried farther?** Gill notes a rabbinic debate: Jarchi (Rashi) thought the weeping was heard farther; Gill thinks the shouting of the younger, more numerous crowd prevailed at a distance. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/3.htm)
- **Matthew Henry's pastoral application.** "They despised the day of small things, and were unthankful for the good they enjoyed. Let not the remembrance of former afflictions drown the sense of present mercies." Yet he also grants the old men had reason to weep: "if they bewailed the sin that was the cause of this melancholy change, they did well." (Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezra/3.htm)

## Denominational & Other Perspectives

### Reformed (Ligonier.org)
- The Jews rebuilt the altar out of both fear and faith — "Their awareness of their vulnerability…encouraged them to get the job done. At the altar, they could meet with the Lord and call on His name for protection." The foundation ceremony shows that from "small beginnings He delights to bring greater glory" — a call not to "despise what seem to be 'small' moves of God." (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/rebuilding-the-temple)
- Another Ligonier devotional notes that the people "did not see the spectacular new beginning they had hoped for but a building so pitiful in comparison to Solomon's temple that it made those who had seen the former temple mourn bitterly." (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/foolish-priorities)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
- Guzik applies the altar-first principle to the Christian life: "We have an altar (Hebrews 13:10), the cross of Jesus Christ, set upon its ancient foundations. The altar was to them what the cross is to Christians under the new covenant." He warns against "the backward look which discounts present activity" — "regrets over the past that paralyse work in the present are always wrong." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-3/)

### Evangelical / Bible.org tradition (Precept Austin citing Steven Cole)
- Cole structures the chapter around "New Beginnings with God." Key points: (1) New beginnings are possible no matter how spiritually low we have gone. (2) They must focus on the cross (the altar as type of Christ's sacrifice). (3) They must focus on obedience to God's Word ("as it is written" repeated). (4) They must focus on building God's house — which requires courage, sacrificial giving, unity under godly leadership, and cooperation between old and young. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-3-commentary)

### Dispensational / Bible Exposition (Gaebelein, Constable, Bell)
- Gaebelein sees a spiritual order: "the building of the altar-worship; obedience to the Word of God, and then whole-souled and united service for the Lord. This is the order still for God's people." He also draws a parallel to present church conditions: "when we too remember the former things and present conditions in the ruin and confusion all around us in that which professes His Name, we also weep. And yet we shout and praise Him when we remember His mercy, which endureth forever." (Gaebelein via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/ezra-3.html)
- Constable notes that in offering burnt offerings before the temple foundation was laid, the Jews "showed their earnest desire to be living sacrifices to Him" — connecting the burnt offering to Romans 12:1. (Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezra-3.html)
